article.plain_text:
Which sites ran the same trials, and who has a stake in the answer?
TLDR: Too Long, Did Not Read Answer is Probably Not.
I will start this off with the fact that I am obviously biased, but at the same time I am on the record for discussing some of the benefits that  private equity is hopefully bringing to our industry. It is becoming clear to me that the private equity backed site networks want, no, NEED, more market share and the feasibility surveys are Exhibit A.  At Yuma Clinical Trials, an independent community-based site, the people who answer the feasibility survey are the people who screen and randomize the patients. On one study we read the eligibility criteria and figured we could enroll 20 to 25 in about six months. After the sponsor turned us down, they told me the plan was five sites at 60 patients apiece because that is what some site networks promised. I’d answered their question. I wish I’d asked how many sites they planned to open.
That was a foreshadowing. The chart I saw on LinkedIn this morning was about patients who actually finished trials. Completion is the culmination of patient retention, one of the things independent sites actually do well in my opinion. I guess we are at Exhibit B now. Tufts reported average completion of 80.2% at network-affiliated sites, 41.8% in its combined independent and part-time group, and 24.0% at academic medical centers.
 
This chart is impressive
 
I believe those are the averages they saw. We are now left to wonder (after being impressed by a multitude of random statistics) how much of the gap would survive if both teams ran the same study, head to head comparisons, using the same initial raw data? Here is the link to the study if you want to be bedazzled.
Read the Association of Multisite Research Corporations caption alongside the graphic. The bar says “Independent AND part-time.” The caption turns that into 42% “for independent sites” and asks what full integration might deliver “if network affiliation alone moves performance this far.” Translation: How much better things could be sponsor if you ONLY used private equity backed site networks! 
great caption!
Drop “and part-time” and you’ve given my dedicated research site as well as every other private community based independent site a performance record the authors never measured separately for reasons unbeknownst to any of us yet we are supposed to go along with it like it is Gospel.
Where the headline came from
Ten sponsors and CROs took part in this "study". The authors describe 857 sites across 15 studies, with some performance data from 693 sites. Table 10’s three site-type counts add up to 693. In Table 11, the three completion counts add up to 463. Completion means that a randomized patient finished the study. The article supplies no patient totals behind the site averages.
 
Table 10
 
Table 11
March/April report and definitions
How two groups can tie on each trial and finish 36 points apart
I give Tufts credit for getting sponsors and CROs to share operating data that site owners rarely get to see. Each contributor supplied site- and protocol-level information from one to three studies. The authors call the small sponsor sample their main limitation. They never say how they selected the protocols or how many had completion data from both groups. That overlap matters. I’d like to see head-to-head completion rates within each trial where both groups supplied data. If there were too few such trials, say so. That would have been an easier and more fair comparison although I suspect those results did not generate the headline numbers they were going for, but that is purely speculation on my part.
Here is why that head-to-head comparison matters. Imagine two protocols with ten randomized patients at every site. On Protocol A, lets say a 2 visit vaccine study that is relatively simple,  nine out of ten patients finish at every location. On Protocol B, lets say a 96 week heart failure trial that is far more complex, three out of ten finish at every location.
Protocol A · 90% finish at every site: Network sites: 8 sites; Unaffiliated sites: 2 sites.
Protocol B · 30% finish at every site: Network sites: 2 sites; Unaffiliated sites: 8 sites.
Total patients who finish: Network sites: 78 of 100; Unaffiliated sites: 42 of 100.
Where did the 36-point lead come from? Network sites enrolled 80 of their 100 patients in the trial that was easier to finish. Independent sites enrolled 80 of theirs in the harder trial. On the vaccine study, both groups finished at 90%. On the heart failure trial, both finished at 30%. The entire gap came from which trials the sites ran.
I made up these numbers. They illustrate the mistake Darrell Huff describes in “Post Hoc Rides Again,” a chapter in How to Lie with Statistics. Give network affiliation credit for those 36 points and you’ve credited it with an advantage that does not exist if you were to  compare sites on the same trial (which still has me scratching my head as to why that was not done).
That’s what I wanted Tufts to publish. On the same protocols where dedicated independent sites and network sites both enrolled patients, how many did each group randomize, and how many finished? The network advantage might still hold up, who knows? Anecdotally I think they would both have similar completers across the board for what it's worth, but I'm just a Youtuber and site owner, not a think tank. Unfortunately, the published study does not answer that question even though I think it could/should.
The concern has a clinical basis. In a separate Tufts study, phase II and III oncology protocols averaged 31.4% completion versus 80.0% for non-oncology. That benchmark used patients enrolled as its denominator. In the landscape survey, 61.0% of network respondents reported vaccine work, compared with 15.3% of academic respondents. The oncology difference was much smaller. It was 29.9% in networks and 35.1% at academic centers. Those were survey respondents. Table 11 I posted above separately says 16% of network sites were in vaccine trials. It never gives the vaccine share of the 23 sites reporting completion. Protocol mix is a credible explanation whose contribution we can’t quantify, and it may also be a reason for why they made this analysis so complex in trying to answer two questions as opposed to the headline grabbing one.
Tufts never tells us how many of the 23 network sites reporting completion were running vaccine trials. That matters because the mix of protocols could explain some or all of the gap. To answer the question raised by the headline, we didn’t need Claude. Sponsors and CROs had already supplied site- and protocol-level performance data. What I wanted to see was how many patients finished at each type of site on the same trial. If too few trials had completion data from both groups, say so. Claude came in because Tufts also wanted to answer a different question about how much trial activity each type of site accounts for. It helped build a list of networks and academic centers so the researchers could classify FDA investigator records. That may help estimate where the work goes. It still leaves a reader wondering whether a network site would retain more patients on the particular trial it’s trying to place.
What the statistical test can answer
Tufts reports a p-value below 0.001 for completion across all three site groups. That tells us there’s evidence that at least one group’s average differed from the others. The specific head-to-head result the authors highlight is for screen failure. On completion, they never tell us how large the gap was between network and unaffiliated sites running the same protocol, or give a confidence interval for that gap.
That distinction matters. Sites on the same trial follow the same eligibility criteria and visit schedule. Several of the 23 network sites could also belong to one company and share staff or systems. The article doesn’t say how many owners those sites represent or how the analysis accounted for those ties. Even on the same protocol, sponsors choose which sites participate, and those sites may draw patients from different referral sources. Patients were randomized to treatment. Nobody randomly assigned the clinics to join a network.
My bet is that dedicated independent sites and network sites would have similar completion rates head to head. I’d challenge the authors to show us how many patients each group randomized and how many finished on the protocols they had in common. If the network advantage holds up, I want to know by how much. And since sponsors also care about enrollment, I’d ask one separate question: what percentage of sites in each group actually met the enrollment target they agreed to?
Which patients and sites counted
Darrell Huff describes a neighborhood with a mean family income of $15,000 and a median of $3,500. In my two-clinic example, one finishes 2 of 2 patients and the other finishes 4 of 8. The mean and median site rates are both 75%. Across patients, 6 of 10 finished, or 60%. Now let me pick which clinic to call the network after I see the scores. I can make either group win. In a real study, somebody else ought to be able to check how each clinic got its label.
Darrell Huff, How to Lie with Statistics, illustrated by Irving Geis (W. W. Norton, 1954), chapters 2, 7, 8 and 10. Book and chapter list
Who counts as an independent site
On the same protocol, say a full-time network site and a full-time independent each finish 8 of 10 patients. An unaffiliated part-time practice finishes 4 of 10. The dedicated sites tied, yet the published grouping would give networks an 80% to 60% lead. If all ten at the part-time practice finish, the combined group wins 90% to 80%. Tufts gives us no separate rate for dedicated independents and one has to wonder why.
The March/April report found the same ordering, with 70.6%, 31.3% and 21.5% for networks, the combined group and academic centers respectively. Its performance table covered 12 phase II/III studies and 524 sites. The authors, survey dates and response count line up with October. The reports don’t reconcile which performance records overlap. I take the consistency seriously, but I would want an independently assembled sample before treating it as replication and I would hope study sponsors are just as discerning.
How 1,154 replies became a market-share estimate
I understand why Tufts went beyond the sponsor data. Fifteen selected protocols can tell you something about those studies. They give you no reliable way to count how much work each kind of site does worldwide. For that question the researchers used a site survey and FDA investigator records. Sponsors supplied the patient completion figures separately. The issue I have is that the market-share analysis does not establish that site networks retain more patients. That question needs a comparison of completion rates within the same trials.
The survey got 1,154 replies from people. To estimate how many physical sites they represented, Tufts looked for matches on geography, ownership, network status, first study year and rare-disease work. It allowed annual volumes to differ by up to ten trials and required at least 80% overlap in the listed therapeutic areas and phases. Two coordinators at Yuma Clinical Trials could remember our first study year differently and get counted separately. Two sister network clinics with similar answers could get combined. The article reports no check against known site identities.
The matching exercise produced an estimate of 1,090 sites. Look at the next table.
 
Table 2
Its three counts are 555, 522 and 77. They add to 1,154, and 77 divided by 1,154 gives the published 6.7%. Where did the 64 extra replies fall? If a network and an unaffiliated practice each did one survey per location, but several people at one university answered, the university would get extra weight. The reverse is possible. Tufts gives no count of distinct sites by segment, response rate or check against the population of eligible sites. Even perfect matching would leave the question of who chose to respond.
Here is the multiplication behind Table 2. Weight each group’s replies by its average number of principal investigators (PIs) per site and by the FDA-derived activity per PI over five years. The last column is each group’s result divided by the total across all three.
Academic medical center: Replies: 555; PIs/site × activity/PI: 8.26 × 2.31; Share: 53.8%.
Independent and part-time: Replies: 522; PIs/site × activity/PI: 4.67 × 2.89; Share: 35.8%.
Network-affiliated: Replies: 77; PIs/site × activity/PI: 5.67 × 4.68; Share: 10.4%.
For networks, 77 × 5.67 × 4.68 gives roughly 2,043 units of estimated activity. The three groups total about 19,678. Divide 2,043 by 19,678 and you get 10.4%. I can reproduce all three percentages from the printed inputs. Networks come out above their share of replies because their modeled activity per site is higher. That advantage is already in the inputs.
Again, the point of all of this was never to address the headline question of which site type has a higher patient completion rate. A within-trial comparison wherever both groups supplied completion data would give us a better clue. We don’t know how many of the 15 trials would qualify. Sometimes more data raises more questions than it purportedly answers, and this seems to be a chronic condition of the clinical research industry as a whole.
Tufts used Claude to help generate a list of network and academic names for matching FDA records. People reviewed the list and used text rules such as “University” to label records. If a network buys a clinic that keeps its local name, the match can miss it. Assigning a clinic’s earlier filings to its current owner could also credit a buyer for work done before the sale. Tufts gives no validation against dated affiliations. The survey matching and the sponsor completion analysis are separate from this AI step.
The authors and their financial relationships
Darrell Huff asks “Who says so?” I’m a site owner with a YouTube channel dedicated to smaller sites, I've already admitted my bias but I think we should have a fair comparison. I see the feasibility surveys that reach Yuma, and my business has money riding on the answers. When a sponsor passes on us, I rarely get to see how the winning site did, although occasionally we get asked to come on as a rescue site because I guess other sites didn't fulfill their promises, but I digress. I’d like the same candor from the people behind this research. The clearest author-level relationship I could document was Kenneth Getz’s board appointment at WCG, a company that offers network affiliation to independent sites amongst a slew of other services including centralized IRB offerings.
Kenneth Getz
Getz directs Tufts CSDD. WCG announced his appointment to its board of directors in December 2023, and WCG’s 2025 conference biography still identified him as a board member in the year the survey was fielded. WCG offers independent sites nonexclusive network affiliation and markets its network to sponsors. Private equity firm Arsenal Capital Partners lists WCG in its healthcare portfolio. Sponsors’ willingness to route studies through networks matters to a company selling that service. The October guest column mentions Getz’s board appointments generally. I could not verify his board status on publication day, his compensation or equity, or whether WCG contributed funds or data to this project.
Joan Chambers and Abigail Dirks
Chambers is a senior consultant advising research and membership programs. Tufts names her as the contact for its Circle of Supporters. Annual sponsors may discuss findings with faculty, help identify research priorities and receive member rates on working-group studies. Earlier in her career, Chambers was VP of marketing and strategy at Clin-X, whose affiliated businesses included ClinEdge and BTC Network. That history is relevant experience. It does not establish a continuing financial stake. Dirks is the center’s senior data scientist and first-listed author. I found no public evidence of a personal PE payment or network ownership interest tied to this study for either.
How sponsors help shape the work
Tufts says private-sector grants cover roughly 55% of center operating expenses in a typical year and public-sector grants about 45%. The center also receives course and subscription fees. Grant examples include ICON, IQVIA, Parexel and Pfizer. Those are center-wide disclosures. I could not verify the funders or dollar amounts for this study. The ten organizations that contributed data cannot automatically be counted as ten financial sponsors.
Tufts says its faculty and director set the research agenda. Its announcement of this project says working-group companies help shape hypotheses and methods and review and interpret findings. Participants can also receive custom benchmarking reports. That structure gives the center an incentive to produce work its industry partners value. Access to operational data is a real benefit of the arrangement. The disclosure I want is who chose the protocols, who paid, who saw the analysis before publication and who had approval rights. I found no evidence that any author was paid to deliver a favorable result for private equity, but as an independent community-based site owner, I am sure I am speaking for myself and others when I want to make sure that we are being measured on an even playing field when these types of influential "studies" are being distributed to sponsors who have to decide on utilizing more site networks or independent sites. Ultimately every sponsor makes their own call, but in my opinion, this particular study was an unfair representation of independent sites.
Who benefits when the chart reaches a sponsor
Clinical Leader published the Tufts article as a guest column. Its parent, Life Science Connect, received an investment from Latticework Capital Management and Edgehill Management. Latticework describes the publisher as a marketing and lead-generation business. It also formed American Clinical Research Services, which acquired multisite operator Elixia. One investor backed both the publisher and a company competing for clinical trial work. I found no public evidence that Latticework commissioned, edited or paid for the Tufts article.
AMRC’s incentive is more direct. Its membership is open to corporations that wholly own at least five sites. Sponsors directing more work to those companies serves its members. NMS Capital says member Flourish Research made eleven acquisitions and grew revenue more than tenfold before NMS sold it to Genstar. AMRC’s FY2025 tax-return summary records $406,251 in contributions and grants, without identifying the individual payers. Clinical Leader distributed an earlier AMRC survey, and its chief editor also moderated an AMRC panel that included a skeptical independent operator. Tufts and AMRC are listed as collaborators on a separate sponsor-performance project. These are documented business relationships. They leave the funding of the October study open.
Tufts never breaks out completion rates by private equity ownership. The authors call the small sponsor sample their biggest limitation and warn that investor pressure could affect patient engagement. AMRC goes further and gives network affiliation itself credit for the gap.
I’ll give the PE-backed networks credit where I’ve seen them earn it. If I’m a sponsor trying to open five sites, I see the appeal of negotiating one contract and having a dedicated regulatory team get all five moving. That competition has pushed those of us running independent sites to get faster, too. At Yuma, we can show a sponsor how long it takes us to open a study, enter a visit and answer a data query. I think networks have helped raise that standard.
Where I part company with AMRC is patient completion. If a PE-backed network pays a premium for an independent site, part of what it may be buying is a coordinator who already knows the patients and has spent years getting them back for follow-up. That team’s track record is one reason the site is worth buying. I’d like to see what patients at that same site did on comparable trials before and after the acquisition. Then we could start to see how much the network added to what it bought.
If I’m asking Tufts to show its work, I think we ought to show ours. I’d like our SOS Save Our Sites community to partner with sponsors willing to compare dedicated independent sites and network sites on the same trials. Pick the measures up front. How long did it take each site to open? Of the patients each site randomized, how many completed the study, and how many provided the primary endpoint? Collect both measures using definitions agreed up front, along with the reasons patients did not complete. Maybe survey some monitors. Then publish what we find, whichever way it goes.
I know sites like mine do better than that 42% headline suggests. I’ve got 22 years of experience behind that opinion. What I’d like to put behind it now is data a sponsor can use the next time it has to choose a site, but at the very least, provide some healthy skepticism to the industry for scrutinizing the headlines, following the money, and looking at the details because as Darrell Huff warned us more than half a century ago, it is very easy to "Lie With Statistics".  I guess for myself as well as us small site owners, we gotta get used to continuing to punch above our weight class this next decade.
